lead: Loss sets how far a link reaches; rise time sets how fast it can run. Each part of the link slows the edges of a pulse, and a pulse that spreads too much runs into its neighbour. The rise-time budget adds these slowdowns and compares the total with the bit period. With the power budget it gives two maximum lengths, one set by attenuation and one by dispersion; the shorter is the real reach.
prereq: You need the link power budget, and modal and chromatic dispersion in fibers.

blocks.text: A rise time is the 10 % to 90 % time of a step response. Four independent slowdowns act: the transmitter (t<sub>tx</sub>), modal dispersion (t<sub>mod</sub>), chromatic dispersion (t<sub>chrom</sub>) and the receiver (t<sub>rx</sub>). For near-Gaussian responses they add in quadrature:

blocks.where: t<sub>sys</sub> is the system rise time; all four terms in the same unit (ns or ps).

blocks.text: With bit period T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B, the rule is t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.7T<sub>b</sub> for NRZ and t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.35T<sub>b</sub> for RZ, whose pulse fills only half the slot. Turned round, the highest bit rate is B<sub>max</sub> = 0.7/t<sub>sys</sub> (NRZ) or 0.35/t<sub>sys</sub> (RZ). Some syllabi call this the bandwidth budget.

items: Transmitter ttx. From the data sheet: a few ns for an LED, tens to hundreds of ps for a laser.
Receiver trx. trx = 350/Brx ns, with Brx the receiver's 3 dB bandwidth in MHz.
Modal tmod. Multimode fiber only: tmod = 440 Lq/B0 ns, with B0 the bandwidth of 1 km in MHz·km and L in km. Mode mixing makes q lie between 0.5 and 1 (0.7 is typical). Zero in single-mode fiber.

Chromatic tchrom. Every fiber: tchrom = |D| L σλ, with D in ps/(nm·km), L in km and σλ the source spectral width in nm (the half-power width in most link-design texts; use the width the question gives).

blocks.text: The source width dominates. Over 20 km at 1550 nm (D = 17 ps/(nm·km)) a 2 nm Fabry–Perot laser gives 680 ps but a 0.1 nm DFB laser 34 ps; a 40 nm LED at 850 nm (|D| ≈ 90 ps/(nm·km)) gives 18 ns over just 5 km.

Solving the power budget for L gives the attenuation limit L<sub>att</sub> = (P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> − joint losses − M) ÷ α: with 28 dB available, no joints or margin and 0.22 dB/km, 127 km. It is flat in B for a fixed receiver; real sensitivity worsens as B rises, so it falls slowly.

The dispersion limit is where the fiber term uses up the allowance: L<sub>disp</sub> = √((0.7/B)² − t<sub>tx</sub>² − t<sub>rx</sub>²) ÷ (|D|σ<sub>λ</sub>) for single-mode fiber. Ignoring t<sub>tx</sub> and t<sub>rx</sub> gives the quick bound L<sub>disp</sub> ≈ 0.7/(B|D|σ<sub>λ</sub>), falling as 1/B: 20.6 km at 1 Gbit/s for |D|σ<sub>λ</sub> = 34 ps/km (Fabry–Perot), 412 km for 1.7 ps/km (DFB).

The reach is the smaller of the two: loss wins at low bit rates, dispersion at high ones, crossing near 160 Mbit/s for the Fabry–Perot laser and 3.2 Gbit/s for the DFB. A dispersion-limited link needs a narrower source or a wavelength nearer the zero-dispersion point; a loss-limited one needs more power, a better receiver or an amplifier.

figure.caption: The loss limit (127 km for 28 dB at 0.22 dB/km) against the dispersion limits 0.7/(B|D|σ<sub>λ</sub>) at D = 17 ps/(nm·km). A 2 nm Fabry–Perot laser crosses the loss line at 0.16 Gbit/s; at 1 Gbit/s it allows 20.6 km, and 16.2 km once the transmitter and receiver rise times are counted.

spec.aria: Log-log graph of maximum length in kilometres against bit rate from 0.1 to 10 gigabits per second. A flat line at 127 km for the loss limit, a falling line for a 2 nanometre Fabry-Perot laser and a dashed falling line for a 0.1 nanometre DFB laser. Crossings at 0.16 and 3.2 gigabits per second; points at 20.6 and 16.2 km at 1 gigabit per second.

examples.question: A 20 Mbit/s NRZ link runs 5 km over graded-index multimode fiber at 850 nm. The LED has a rise time of 12 ns and a spectral width of 40 nm. The fiber has |D| = 90 ps/(nm·km) and B<sub>0</sub> = 500 MHz·km (take q = 0.7). The receiver bandwidth is 30 MHz. Does the link pass the rise-time budget? Find the highest NRZ and RZ bit rates it can carry.
steps: Allowed: T<sub>b</sub> = 1/(20 × 10⁶) = 50 ns, so t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 35 ns.
24.7 ns ≤ 35 ns: it passes, and the LED's spectral width is the largest term.
Highest bit rates: NRZ B<sub>max</sub> = 0.7 ÷ 24.7 ns = 28.3 Mbit/s; RZ B<sub>max</sub> = 0.35 ÷ 24.7 ns = 14.2 Mbit/s.
examples.answer: It passes (24.7 ns against 35 ns), and carries up to 28.3 Mbit/s NRZ or 14.2 Mbit/s RZ, so RZ at 20 Mbit/s would fail.

examples.question: A 1 Gbit/s NRZ link uses 20 km of standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm (D = 17 ps/(nm·km)) and a Fabry–Perot laser of spectral width 2 nm. The transmitter rise time is 250 ps and the receiver rise time 350 ps. The launched power is 0 dBm, the sensitivity −28 dBm, α = 0.22 dB/km, with no joints or margin. Does the link pass? If not, find the longest fiber the rise-time budget allows and compare it with the attenuation limit.
steps: Allowed: T<sub>b</sub> = 1000 ps, so t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 700 ps. t<sub>chrom</sub> = 17 × 20 × 2 = 680 ps; t<sub>mod</sub> = 0.
t<sub>sys</sub> = √(250² + 680² + 350²) = √647 400 = 804.6 ps > 700 ps: it fails, and could carry only 0.7 ÷ 804.6 ps = 0.87 Gbit/s NRZ.
Longest length from rise time: L = 552.3 ÷ (17 × 2) = 16.2 km.
Attenuation limit: L<sub>att</sub> = 28 ÷ 0.22 = 127 km. At 20 km the fiber loses only 4.4 dB of the 28 dB available.
examples.answer: It fails (804.6 ps against 700 ps). Rise time limits the reach to 16.2 km, far below the 127 km loss limit; a 0.1 nm DFB laser (34 ps) would pass.

traps: Adding rise times directly: 12 + 2.7 + 18 + 11.7 = 44.4 ns would wrongly fail the first example.
Using 0.7T<sub>b</sub> for RZ. RZ allows only 0.35T<sub>b</sub>.
Mixing units: t<sub>rx</sub> = 350/B<sub>rx</sub> gives ns only with B<sub>rx</sub> in MHz; D in ps/(nm·km) gives t<sub>chrom</sub> in ps.
Quoting the dispersion limit alone as the reach. The reach is the smaller of L<sub>att</sub> and L<sub>disp</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the rise-time budget condition for an NRZ link.
quiz.a: t<sub>sys</sub> = √(t<sub>tx</sub>² + t<sub>mod</sub>² + t<sub>chrom</sub>² + t<sub>rx</sub>²) ≤ 0.7T<sub>b</sub>, with T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B.

quiz.q: Why are rise times added in quadrature and not directly?
quiz.a: For independent, near-Gaussian responses the variances (squares of the widths) add, so the total is the root of the sum of squares.

quiz.q: A 2.5 Gbit/s NRZ link has t<sub>tx</sub> = 100 ps, t<sub>rx</sub> = 200 ps and a fiber rise time of 400 ps. Does it pass, and what is its highest NRZ bit rate?
quiz.a: T<sub>b</sub> = 400 ps, allowance 280 ps. t<sub>sys</sub> = √(100² + 400² + 200²) = √210 000 = 458.3 ps > 280 ps: it fails. B<sub>max</sub> = 0.7 ÷ 458.3 ps = 1.53 Gbit/s.

quiz.q: Estimate the dispersion-limited length at 10 Gbit/s for D = 17 ps/(nm·km) and σ<sub>λ</sub> = 0.1 nm, ignoring the transmitter and receiver.
A link has L<sub>att</sub> = 80 km and L<sub>disp</sub> = 120 km at 2 Gbit/s. What is its reach, and what happens at 4 Gbit/s?
quiz.a: 80 km, set by loss. L<sub>disp</sub> falls as 1/B to 60 km at 4 Gbit/s, so dispersion binds and the reach is 60 km.
A first-order low-pass response has a 10 to 90 % rise time of 2.2RC = 0.35/B<sub>rx</sub>; with B<sub>rx</sub> in MHz this is 350/B<sub>rx</sub> ns.

quiz.q: Why can a link pass the power budget but fail the rise-time budget?
quiz.a: Loss and spreading are separate: the 20 km, 1 Gbit/s example loses only 4.4 dB but spreads to 804.6 ps because the source is wide.

beyond: Coherent receivers now undo chromatic dispersion in digital signal processing, so high-speed channels cross long distances without optical compensation. Search for electronic dispersion compensation to go further.
